opus-5.5.text:
FP8 is one of those things that sounds like a small engineering detail but can matter a lot at scale. The basic promise is simple: lower precision means you move less memory and get more throughput from the hardware, so for the same compute budget you can train bigger models or train longer on more tokens. When you're spending tens of millions of dollars on a single run, even a 30 or 40 percent efficiency gain adds up fast.

The hard part is stability. When we scaled up, we kept seeing that precision issues which barely show up at small scale start hurting you at large scale. You get outliers in activations, loss spikes, divergence late in training, and those are very expensive to discover after weeks of compute. So FP8 isn't a free lunch. You need careful scaling factors, you have to decide which operations stay in higher precision, and you need a lot of monitoring.

So my view is that it's very promising, and I think it'll become standard, the same way BF16 did. But the gains don't come from flipping a switch. They come from co-designing the recipe, the architecture, and the infrastructure together. Teams that invest in making low precision robust will get a real edge, not just because each run is cheaper, but because they can run more experiments, and in this field iteration speed is everything.

I'd also add that precision is just one lever. Data quality, post-training, and how you use compute at inference time often matter as much or more. FP8 helps you do more with your compute, but you still have to spend that compute on the right things.

r001.rationale: The response describes FP8’s efficiency gains and its potential to support larger or longer training runs, but it does not identify those gains as an advance relative to 32- or 64-bit training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so FP8 is one of those things where the promise is very clear on paper and the reality is a bit more subtle. The promise is basically a 2x on compute throughput compared to BF16, and when you're spending tens of thousands of GPUs for months, 2x is enormous. That's not a small optimization, that's the difference between one model and two models for the same budget.

But the reason it hasn't been the default yet is stability. When we trained Llama 2 and Llama 3, we were already seeing loss spikes, divergences, things that are hard to debug at scale. BF16 is forgiving. FP8 is not. You have a very narrow dynamic range, so you need per-tensor or even per-block scaling, you need to be careful about which operations stay in higher precision, the optimizer states, the gradients accumulation, the attention softmax. If you get any of that wrong, the training looks fine for a few hundred billion tokens and then it quietly degrades, or it blows up. And when you're training at frontier scale, you don't get to restart five times. So the risk-adjusted calculation matters a lot. It's not just "is it 2x faster", it's "what is the probability I lose two weeks of compute".

What changed my view is seeing people actually ship with it. DeepSeek-V3 is the obvious example, they did most of the matmuls in FP8 with fine-grained scaling and it worked, and they were very open about the recipe. That was important for the community because it de-risked it. Before that, a lot of labs had FP8 working in experiments but nobody wanted to be the first to bet a flagship run on it.

So my view today is that it's inevitable. It's going to become the default the same way BF16 replaced FP32 mixed precision. And then the next frontier is FP4, which NVIDIA is pushing hard with Blackwell, and there the question is even more interesting because at some point you're really asking how much noise can gradient descent tolerate, and the answer seems to be, more than we thought.

The thing I'd add is that the hardware is forcing the question. If the hardware gives you 2x or 4x for lower precision, you can't ignore it, because your competitors won't. So the research direction becomes less "should we do it" and more "how do we make the training algorithms robust enough so that it doesn't matter". Things like better normalization, better initialization, stochastic rounding, and honestly just more engineering discipline in monitoring the run so you catch problems early.

r001.rationale: The response describes FP8 as a major scaling opportunity and claims 2× throughput over BF16, but it does not identify an FP8 advantage relative to 32- or 64-bit training. FP32 is mentioned only in the comparison of BF16’s adoption.

astra-6.text:
I think FP8 is a promising way to make scaling more efficient. If you can reduce the precision you use during training while preserving the quality of the model, you can reduce memory usage and increase throughput. That means you can do more experiments or train a larger model with the same compute budget.

The challenge is numerical stability. It’s not simply a matter of switching everything to eight bits. You need to understand which operations can tolerate lower precision and which still need higher precision. And you need to verify that the gains hold over a full training run, not just in a short benchmark.

So I’m optimistic, but the metric that matters is how much compute it takes to reach a given model quality. If FP8 improves that reliably, it becomes a very useful tool for scaling.

r001.rationale: The response describes FP8 as promising and says it could support larger models or more experiments with the same compute budget, but it does not identify FP8 as a substantial advance relative to 32- or 64-bit training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think FP8 is a promising way to make scaling more efficient. If you can reduce the precision while preserving training stability and model quality, you can lower memory usage and get more compute out of the same hardware. That could let you train a larger model, or run more experiments, within the same budget.

But the important question is whether those gains hold across an entire training run. You have to be careful about numerical stability, and you may still need higher precision for some operations. So I see a lot of potential, but the real measure is the end-to-end improvement at the same quality—not just the theoretical throughput.

r001.rationale: The response describes FP8 as promising for more efficient scaling, but does not identify it as a substantial advance relative to 32- or 64-bit training.
